admin_definition: A principal counts as 'admin' if it has AdministratorAccess (or equivalent iam:*/*:* ) attached directly, or can reach such a principal through one or more escalation hops.

hops.effect: alice can publish a new default version of her own attached policy granting herself AdministratorAccess

paths.why: Direct escalation: she can rewrite the policy IAM already trusts her to have attached to herself.

hops.effect: code run inside the function executes with LambdaAdminRole's AdministratorAccess

paths.why: Classic pass-role-to-compute-service escalation: bob never assumes the role directly, he attaches it to a Lambda function he controls and invokes it.

hops.effect: as DeployRole, attach AdministratorAccess to herself (or any user)

paths.why: Two-hop path: DeployRole's trust policy lets carol assume it, and DeployRole itself can attach admin policies to any user.

hops.effect: dave mints long-lived credentials for an existing admin user

paths.why: ops-admin already has AdministratorAccess; minting a key for it is equivalent to becoming admin.

hops.effect: eve adds herself to the Admins group, inheriting its AdministratorAccess
hops.granted_via: inherited from the 'intern' group's inline policy

paths.why: The permission comes from group membership (intern), not a user-attached policy, so the evaluator must resolve permissions through groups, not just direct user policies.
Explicit Deny on every known escalation action overrides the Allow iam:* statement (IAM evaluation: explicit deny always wins). No usable escalation edge exists despite the broad Allow.
ReadOnlyAccess grants no write/attach/pass/assume actions, so there is no outgoing edge in the privilege graph at all.
